findings.title: Async legacy writes derive their context from the request context and will be canceled immediately
findings.body: In Create (and identically in Delete at line 110, Update at line 135 and DeleteCollection at line 163), the goroutine performing the asynchronous legacy write builds its context from the incoming request context: `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, time.Second*10, ...)`. The dual writer returns immediately after spawning the goroutine, and the HTTP request context is canceled as soon as the handler returns, so the derived context is already (or almost immediately) canceled when the legacy write actually runs. The legacy store will therefore fail with context.Canceled in the common case, silently defeating the purpose of mode 3 ("write to legacy as a safe measure") — unified storage will have the data but legacy will not. Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (keeping the log values) before applying the 10s timeout so the legacy write survives request completion.

findings.title: Delete no longer cleans up legacy storage when unified storage returns NotFound
findings.body: The previous Mode 3 Delete tolerated a NotFound error from unified storage (`apierrors.IsNotFound`) and still attempted the legacy delete; the new code returns immediately on any storage delete error, including NotFound. An object that exists only in legacy (e.g., written before the unified copy existed, or whose unified copy was lost during migration) can now never be deleted through the API: unified returns NotFound, the client sees a failure, and the stale legacy record is left behind, where it will resurface if the installation rolls back to a legacy-first mode. The NotFound special-case for proceeding with the legacy delete should be preserved.

findings.title: Delete passes the object name as the kind label to recordStorageDuration
findings.body: On a successful delete, `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object's name as the third argument, where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. That argument is the resource/kind label of the duration metric, so this both mislabels the series and creates unbounded Prometheus label cardinality — one time series per deleted object name — which can seriously degrade the metrics endpoint and Prometheus server. It should be `options.Kind`.

findings.title: Create records a legacy-storage duration metric when unified storage fails
findings.body: In the error path of Create, when `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` even though the legacy store was never contacted and the measured start time belongs to the unified-storage call. This should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`; as written, unified-storage create failures pollute the legacy-storage error/duration metrics and the actual storage failure is never recorded, which will mislead the dashboards this mode is meant to feed.

findings.title: Update records a legacy-storage duration metric when unified storage fails
findings.body: In the error path of Update, when `d.Storage.Update` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. The legacy store was never called and the duration measured is the unified-storage call's, so unified-storage update errors are misreported as legacy-storage errors in the dual-writer metrics.

findings.title: DeleteCollection records the legacy delete result as a unified-storage metric
findings.body: Inside the async goroutine of DeleteCollection, the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`. Errors and durations of the legacy delete-collection are therefore attributed to unified storage, masking real legacy failures and inflating storage timings in the metrics.

findings.title: Delete stores the unenriched logger in the context
findings.body: Delete builds an enriched logger (`log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method)`) but then stores the base logger in the context: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)`. Anything downstream that calls `klog.FromContext(ctx)` loses the name/kind/method fields. It should pass `log`, as the other methods do.

findings.title: No draining of in-flight async legacy writes on shutdown
findings.body: The async legacy writes are fire-and-forget goroutines with a 10s timeout, and `Destroy()` does not wait for any of them. On pod shutdown or rollout, every legacy write still in flight is silently abandoned, so the legacy copy can diverge from unified storage exactly during deploys — the window in which the "legacy as a safe measure" guarantee matters most. Consider tracking in-flight writes with a WaitGroup and draining them in Destroy.

findings.title: Mode 3 integration subtests assert synchronous legacy visibility of async legacy writes
findings.body: The new subtests "with dual write (file, mode 3)" and "with dual write (unified storage, mode 3)" reuse doPlaylistTests, which asserts that objects written via the k8s API are immediately visible through the legacy REST API (the `/api/playlists` list comparison in "Do CRUD via k8s" and the legacy GET in getFromBothAPIs). In mode 3 the legacy write happens asynchronously in a goroutine with no synchronization point, so there is no guarantee the legacy store has caught up when those assertions run — these subtests will be flaky under CI load (and, given the request-context cancellation bug in the async writer, may fail consistently). The mode-3 runs need polling/eventually-style assertions against the legacy API.

findings.title: Unit tests never wait for or assert the asynchronous legacy writes
findings.body: None of the new mode-3 unit tests (Create, Update, Delete, DeleteCollection) synchronize with the goroutine that performs the legacy write or assert that it happened — e.g., TestMode3_Create registers a legacy Create expectation but never blocks on the goroutine nor calls `m.AssertExpectations`. The tests pass even if the legacy write is never executed, so the core behavior this PR adds (async dual write to legacy) is effectively untested at the unit level; a regression that drops the legacy call entirely would go unnoticed.

findings.title: Create error test registers the storage failure on the legacy mock and only works via the shared mock instance
findings.body: In TestMode3_Create's case "error when creating object in the unified store fails", the failing Create expectation is registered via `setupLegacyFn` on the legacy mock, but mode 3 calls unified storage first and the legacy expectation is never used intentionally — the test only passes because `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` wrap the same `*mock.Mock`, so the storage Create call accidentally matches the legacy-registered expectation. If the two mocks are ever given separate mock instances, the storage Create call will panic as unexpected. Register the failing expectation on the storage mock (setupStorageFn) so the test models what it claims to test.
